analysis.one_liner: Phases out farm subsidy payments to large farms and redirects savings to food aid, conservation, and deficit reduction.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee markup and no House floor vote before the 110th Congress ended, despite a bipartisan group of 12 original sponsors and 22 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred anyone earning over $200,000 a year from receiving federal farm subsidy payments, phased those payments down sharply by 2012, and repealed the milk price support and sugar import-quota programs. The savings would have been shifted to bigger food stamp benefits, emergency food banks, school fruit and vegetable programs, rural development, and reducing the federal deficit. It was referred to four House committees in June 2007 and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would have saved money from lower farm subsidies and deficit reduction; low-income households, who would have gotten larger food stamp benefits, higher minimum benefits, and protections for military pay and retirement savings; food banks and school children; and rural residents, who would have gained microenterprise grants, broadband loans, and water and waste projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, food stamp households, rural residents

how_it_helps.text: Barred any direct, counter-cyclical, or transition farm payment to an individual or entity whose average adjusted gross income exceeds $200,000, starting after 2007.
Phased direct payments down to 65% in 2008 and 10% by 2012, with those payments deposited into farmer-run risk management accounts instead of paid out as checks.
Repealed the milk price support program and the sugar tariff-rate quota, and replaced commodity marketing loans with a recourse loan program.
Raised food stamp standard deductions and the minimum monthly benefit, excluded combat pay and retirement accounts from income and asset limits, and reauthorized the program through 2012.

Increased funding for the emergency food assistance program (to $220 million in 2008, rising to $245 million by 2011), expanded the fruit and vegetable school snack program, funded farm-to-school and farmers market programs, and created food bank infrastructure and food recovery grants.
Directed that all savings from the bill, measured against the CBO baseline, go to deficit reduction rather than new spending.

analysis.who_pays: Large farm operations receiving subsidy payments, especially those with high incomes; sugar producers, who would lose tariff-rate quota protection and price supports; dairy farmers and processors, who would lose the milk price floor; and crop insurance companies, whose government reimbursement rate would be cut.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large farm subsidy recipients, sugar, dairy

drawbacks.text: Repealing the milk price support program and the sugar tariff-rate quota would remove the price floor and import protection that dairy and sugar producers rely on, exposing them to volatile world prices and import competition.

Cutting direct payments to 10% of current levels by 2012 would shift income risk onto farmers; the replacement risk management accounts only pay out when a farm's revenue falls below 95% of its five-year average, which may not cushion a severe price collapse.
The crop insurance reimbursement cut (from 24.5 to 23.2) would lower payments to insurance companies, which could lead to higher premiums or reduced service for farmers.
While commodity spending is cut, the bill adds new or expanded funding for rural microenterprise, broadband, biorefineries, biomass research, and food programs, partially offsetting the savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: taxpayer money now flows to large farm operations regardless of need, and the bill would have ended that while meaningfully expanding food assistance for low-income people and reducing the deficit. The honest objections are the transition risk for dairy and sugar producers and for smaller commodity farmers who currently depend on the payment system. On balance the bill was a genuine reform attempt with costs concentrated on a relatively small group of subsidy recipients, but it also carried enough new spending that the deficit savings were smaller than the subsidy cuts alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture Committee and three other House committees in June 2007, shuffled to two subcommittees in September, and never received a markup or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Kind (D-WI) introduced the FARM 21 Act on June 14, 2007, joined by 11 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Jeff Flake, Dave Reichert, Mark Kirk, Todd Russell Platts-era members, Jim Petri, Paul Ryan, Christopher Shays, and Rick Smith, and Democrats Joseph Crowley, Shelley Berkley, Peter DeFazio-era members, Jim McDermott, and Earl Blumenauer.

The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor, Foreign Affairs, and Ways and Means Committees, with the Speaker retaining discretion over which provisions each would consider.

On June 27, 2007 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade, and on September 11, 2007 to the Education and Labor subcommittees on Healthy Families and Communities and on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions. No committee reported the bill and no vote ever occurred.
The bill had 22 cosponsors, 16 Democrats and 6 Republicans, but the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large farm subsidy recipients, sugar producers, and dairy interests were better off; Congress instead passed a 2008 farm bill that continued direct payments largely intact. Taxpayers and food stamp recipients gained nothing from the proposed reforms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large farm subsidy recipients and protected commodity producers

for.name: Rep. Ron Kind (D-WI)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FARM 21 Act to cap and phase down farm subsidies and redirect the savings to nutrition, conservation, rural development, and deficit reduction.

for.name: 22 House cosponsors (16 Democrats, 6 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties including members from subsidy-heavy farm states.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Gave the bill no committee markup or vote during the 2007-2008 farm bill reauthoriation; the committee of primary referral reported nothing and the bill died there.

against.name: Commodity subsidy recipients and farm lobby groups
against.role: Recipients of direct payments and price support programs
against.what_they_did: Opposed payment limits and repeal of commodity support programs during the 2008 farm bill debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan from the start: 12 original sponsors split between the parties, and its 22 cosponsors included 16 Democrats and 6 Republicans, while opposition came from the majority party's committee leadership rather than from a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill capped payments at households earning over $200,000 and phased direct payments down to 10% by 2012, ending a system in which large operations receive federal checks regardless of income. Those payments cost taxpayers money with little public benefit.
Repealing the sugar tariff-rate quota and price support programs would end import protection that keeps domestic sugar prices above world levels, which consumers pay for in food prices.

The bill repealed the milk price support program, which would lower milk prices for consumers, but continued Milk Income Loss Contract payments to dairy operators at 90% of prior levels, partially cushioning producers.
Cut the administrative and operating reimbursement rate from 24.5 to 23.2, reducing the guaranteed government payments insurance companies receive for selling federal crop policies.
Funded promotion of fruit and vegetable consumption, expanded the school fruit and vegetable snack program, and supported farm-to-school and farmers market programs, creating new demand for growers.
Extended and expanded biorefinery grants, loans, and loan guarantees, renewable energy system grants, and biomass research funding.
Reauthorized the rural broadband access loan program and directed CCC funds to pending broadband applications, expanding service in areas private providers underserve.

industries.industry: Food banks and emergency food organizations
industries.note: Raised emergency food assistance commodity funding and created food bank infrastructure and fresh-food transportation grant programs.
